messages.author: 5ccb721d28384a05
messages.subject: Keeping shared peptides
parts:
Hello,

I have been looking at my PSM dataset and I have peptides that are matched to more than 1 protein. This is often the case with Histone isoforms which have very similar sequences. The MSstats default code is to remove shared peptides, which for PD analysis is done by information of # Proteins column. As a result, I seem to be loosing lots of information about protein isoforms on histone proteins. Therefore my protein analysis looks like I detect not Histones even though they are highly abundant.

Why is the default set to remove these PSMs and do you think it would be advisable for me to change this to FALSE?

Many thanks

Sam

messages.author: 6597c45f2a31b5d0
messages.subject: Re: Keeping shared peptides
parts:
Hi Sam,

To be honest, this question is a little hard to answer given there is still ongoing research on how to handle peptides that are matched to more than 1 protein.  

What I can say right now is that the default removes these PSMs to prevent double counting of one peptide's abundance toward multiple proteins.  It's not advisable to change it to FALSE because it could introduce another source of error into your analysis, especially since these identifications have a high degree of uncertainty.

In your case, since you know ahead of time which proteins are histones, you could possibly modify the protein IDs of those histone isoforms to share one common ID, and then you can make a conclusion on the differential abundance of histone isoforms overall (this isn't something MSstats supports and would need to be done adhoc, which can cause reproducibility issues)?  But I don't really see a way where you can get to the granularity of each histone isoform's differential abundance without introducing error.  

Thanks,
Tony

messages.author: 5c6e92c10ef28984
messages.subject: Re: Keeping shared peptides
parts:
Hi,

to expand on Tony's answer:
in MSstats there is no point in changing this option, as summarization module will not properly account for the presence of shared peptides. MSstats simply assumes that only unique peptides are used.

There is an alternative (currently unpublished) summarization algorithm implemented elsewhere (MSstatsWeightedSummary) which accounts for shared peptides, but it works best with repeated measures design (but can work with other designs, too). If you'd like to try out this summarization method on your data, I can assist with that.


Kind regards,
Mateusz

messages.author: 5c6e92c10ef28984
messages.subject: Re: Keeping shared peptides
parts:
Hi,


neither really solves the original problem, but Master Protein Accessions uses a form of protein inference, while  Protein Accessions lists all matching proteins IIRC. The latter causes additional segmentation of shared features by creating new labels (concatenations of matching proteins' IDs). It's best to double check the column definitions, though.


Kind regards,
Mateusz
